response.message:
You Did What Now?...

27.06.10199, Harko Village
Feyd-Rautha Harkonnen, Piter de Vries
... And why am I not surprised?
response.subject: [27.06.10199] You did what now?

response.message:
“But if you desire dames like consuming flames, try a Caladanian daughter,” Feyd hummed dreamily while a naked slave girl washed the desert dust off him. The shortage of water on Arrakis did nothing to reduce the love that Na-Baron had for long, lazy baths, the ones than required hot water added several times. If anything, knowing that people outside would kill each other for much less gave a simple relaxation that touch of proper decadence which all Harkonnens enjoyed and respected.

The bathtub in his suite in Harko was not nearly as opulent as the one Feyd had in Barony, but it still was spacious enough to comfortably fit two people, Feyd’s pale skin against the girl’s olive one. When they were standing, the pleasingly curvy girl barely reached his shoulder, but now, when she was sitting in his lap, it was convenient for them to exchange kisses and Feyd could clearly see the pure admiration in her doe eyes as she ran her soft hands along his muscles. She was perfectly trained in all the skills and deceptions required to provide pleasure. Feyd had bought the girl during his last visit to Kaitain as a souvenir for his brother who rarely received such fine treats, but decided on the way back that she was too fine for Glossu and kept the girl for himself. If the Beast was not pleased with the new lasgun he received instead, he knew better than to show it.

There was another woman Feyd would have preferred to fuck, but that one – she’ll do to calm his thoughts, still swarming with impressions he could not quite put in words. He liked the chase, yes; Ariste deserved to be put in her place which was in his bedroom, yes; there were advantages to making this marriage happen at least under the pretense of free will, too; but there was something else, like a lost memory or a déjà vu, that Feyd did not want to dwell on but could not exorcise from the outskirts of his consciousness where it lurked, a threat and a temptation. He could always drown his doubts in physical sensations, however, and that was what Feyd intended to do, before he was disturbed.

Perhaps, Piter would not have overridden a direct order to not enter the na-baron’s private quarters when the young heir was occupied. It simply had never occurred to Feyd that giving such an order to his guards was an option. When another man appeared, the girl blushed, faking shyness, and leaned closer against Feyd, hiding her breasts from view and nesting her face against his neck. Her wavy brown hair tickled his chin.

“But if you desire dames like consuming flames…” Feyd hummed specially for the mentat, before laughing and saying: “Yes, Piter, I have met with my betrothed. What’s the matter?”

He did not bother to hide that he was well-satisfied with his adventure. Of course, the fact that the Hephaestus, despite being an Atreides trap, still carried Ariste’s personal catspaw, the one her house was unaware of (or ready to sacrifice), was pure luck, but recognizing Ariste’s voice on the comm despite the storm, the hurry to get out and the sounds of the ship blowing up – that was Feyd’s own achievement, as well as memorizing enough details about the degenerate killer, allowing Simona to identify, locate and bug them. Then, of course, there was getting into Arrakeen unrecognized by anyone but his betrothed and wooing that betrothed enough that she did not betray him to the guards. Thrilling! What’s not to like?
response.subject: [27.06.10199] You did what now?

response.message:
Piter walked into Na-Baron’s quarters without spearing the guards a glance. He stopped in the living room for a moment, caught the splash of water in the washing room and walked strait in. He was not in the mood for etiquette. The naked whore was granted one long, piercing glance of deep blue eyes.

“Thirty seconds to disappear.” He was not even talking to her, he was stating a fact. If the clock in his mentat’s head ran before this creature evaporated from the room, he would shoot it. The creature, however, had its wits about it. Or it was simply terrified of his stare - he had that effect on some of the servants. Either way, it took it twenty two seconds to scramble out of Na-Baron’s arms and out of the slippery bathtub and run out of the room. Acceptable. Piter turned around and closed the door behind it.

“The matter is,” he started with that cold, impersonal tone of his he always employed when talking to anyone, but Baron and his victims, “that I can clearly recognize the development of an obsession. As a member of house Harkonnen and a heavy user of spice, I can hardly object to a development of a healthy addiction. That is useful both to you and your Baron. However, obsession is a different matter, Na-Baron. It does not simply put your head at risk. As reckless as you are, you know how to protect your head from the falling debris of a burning spaceship. An obsession, however, raises the question of your priorities. Of your loyalty. To make matters worse, the circumstances of today’s particular burst of your uncontrolled energy look suspicious enough to prove all the charges that could be raised against you. In other words, if someone learns about this insanity of yours, there will be calls to strip you of the Harkonnen name. This girl might be your betrothed, but her house is still the war enemy.”

Piter produced the whole tirade with the same even tone and did not blink once. He knew perfectly well that his words would reach exactly the right spot. The last name of the great house was among the few things that Feyd-Rautha cherished, because he knew it had not been always his. It had been granted to him by his benevolent uncle as a token of trust that he would turn out better than his delusional parents intended. But, while the Baron had never mentioned it out loud, there was always a possibility that the trust would be broken, and the great name would be taken away.

Like his Baron, Piter had never mentioned this option before, but this time, every word of what he had said was real. Young Na-Baron barely had any idea how many people in the house Harkonnen wanted him dead or, at least, removed from the family portraits. Unfortunately for them, the house did not abide by the strict rules of honour, honesty and other nonsense, so it was impossible to accuse one another of smearing the family name and demand their removal on that ground. Addictions, perversions and occasional mass murders were too common in this family to make a fuss about it. There was, however, one thing that could bring a Harkonenn down - an accusation of treason.

Piter could already hear in his head the shouts from the crown at the upcoming family gathering. “The boy has lost his mind over this girl and soon will call himself an Atreidis!” “Just like his father!”
response.subject: [27.06.10199] You did what now?

response.message:
Feyd frowned as he watched the girl scramble away. She had enough sense to remember who her master was and quickly ask for his permission, even if only with her desperate eyes, and he nodded curtly, even knowing that he would not look at her the same afterwards. Maybe Glossu would even get his gift, after all. Despite being the older brother, he was quite used to hand-me-downs. More realistically, however, Feyd’s anger would cool down by then. Piter had done him a favor, in a way, because if the girl had overheard them, he would probably have had to execute her on the spot, and he was not exactly in the mood (though this might change in the course of the conversation).

The first sounds of mentat’s voice did something with Feyd’s expression too. It was sort of a trained response: a reckless youth, chasing for glimpses of freedom in adrenaline spikes, withdrew, the Harkonnen Na-Baron, who had been reflecting the attempts to assassinate or discredit him since he could barely walk, remained and listened intently. He was young and annoyed too, however.

“Girls never liked you, did they, Piter?” As he spoke, Feyd stepped out of the bath, reached for the towel rack and wrapped a towel around his hips, allowing the water to glisten on his muscular body. Even leaning against the tub, he was still taller than Piter. “Not even one? Never ever? Is that it? Your calculation doesn’t compute because you lack the necessary data? Poor, poor Mentat.”

When Feyd was a child, he believed that every word uttered in Piter’s presence ended up in Baron’s ears. By now he had learnt better: his uncle would find out essential things, of course, but the definition of “essential” could be negotiated. His little adventure could still be hushed down. Surely Piter of all people would not actually think him such a fool?

“And maybe I was right, Piter, when I called you poor.” Feyd’s mouth quickly contorted into a sneer so reminiscent of his beloved uncle. His eyes gleamed coldly when he rose his voice. “Why is it that I find out that my betrothed is on Arrakis not from you? Why do you do nothing to prevent an Atreides attempt on my life? Careful, Mentat! I warn you!”

Having let his insolence to sink in, Feyd laughed and moved his hand from the poison darts release button hidden in the edge of the tub.

“But surely you just didn’t want to interfere in such trivial matters. You are very busy, I know, doing great work for our house. And I just had a little chat with my betrothed, that’s all. Her family must be unhappy with me sneaking into their cozy nest, but since when ruffling Atreides feathers a little has become a crime? She was worried that her House would harm me, can you imagine that! If someone’s loyalty here is to be questioned, it is not mine.”

Tutored from infancy by the Mentat, Feyd-Rautha knew how to chase details. You do not force them, you let them enter your awareness at their own time. There was something important in Piter’s long speech. Something useful. What?

“If this House needed a complacent fool to steer it in the future, my brother would still be the heir, not me. I am always mindful of the trust that my uncle placed in me and grateful for all he has done for me. All I do is for the good of House Harkonnen. If there is anyone who doubts it, let them try and take it up with me. I love a little resistance.” He bared his teeth threateningly. He had no friends in this family, he knew. Come to think of it, maybe it would not be such a bad idea to lure some of his enemies out. “Uncle had already signed the agreement and the Emperor ratified it. I would have expected a better match before this war, but now, our losses considered...” Feyd shrugged. All years of planning, undone by Duke’s concubine, considered… Ah. There it was. Obsessions clouding loyalty. Feyd would remember the lesson, in case he ever needs to defend himself against Piter. “All I am doing is ensuring that if we have to uphold this agreement, it works to our profit, not to detriment. Imagine Harkonnens ruling the Caladan Keep! We’d be able to build a power station on the family graveyard to use all the energy from generations of Atreides ancestors turning and rattling their bones in the ground! If it doesn’t come to this, well, knowing the habits and location of Atreides heir would allow us to take her hostage or eliminate her, when needed.” Since you couldn’t be bothered to track her, he left unsaid. “I would not resort to something like that without uncle’s approval, of course.”
response.subject: [27.06.10199] You did what now?

response.message:
Piter let out a heavy sigh. The Na-Baron, while unquestionably promising, was still a spoiled child with annoying mood swings and very childish insults. Piter did not dignify his snarky questions with an answer, although, in fact, they were far from truth. Yet letting the boy know that, in fact, Piter had first spent a night with a girl (and then with a boy, and then with a professor) in much younger age than him, was not going to help this discussion, so he kept silent.

The boy finally stoped posing like an old statue of Atreides ancestors and started thinking out loud. As usual, his thinking was full of somewhat justified arrogance and certain useful details. So Piter's spies were correct, and the Atreides girl had indeed tried to protect Feyd-Rautha from the family guards. It was interesting and could be certainly useful in the future. If only he managed to distract the over-eager Na-Baron from this new pair of milk dispensers for long enough.

"I appreciate that you recognize the work I am doing here, Na-Baron. Certainly, if you stop day dreaming about your love advertures for a moment, you will also recognize that I did not come to make a scene, as it is not my style. I have come to warn you. The Guild-enforced truce agreements and the non-combat zone the Emperor had declared in Hagga Basin are already making the brows rise. The war of Assassins may be much more nuanced than a brute attack by a squad of mindless Sardaukar, yet even then, this war has too many red lines and dragging for far too long. The Landsraat is talking. The Bene Gesserit are trying to worm their way into both camps. The Emperor's counselor is placing his own people in both cities as if we did not have enough spies already. This war is draining us in many more ways than just money and people. It is draining people's sanity, as little of it as most here had in the first place. Compared to all the nonsense going on around, your brother the Beast now looks almost intelligent."

Piter smirked.

"If I am telling you that your escapade will draw attention it is because it will. Everyone is on edge, and the paranoia in the house has become as wild as the worst semuta-infused hallucinations. I can keep the mouths of my own spies shut, or, if needed, their tongs removed, but do not expect that you have only been seen by my people. Unlike Harko, in Arrakeen, Bene Gesserit, desert cultists and who knows what other pests crawl from every crevice with no one to get rid of them. You two have been seen, you may trust my probability calculations on that. So please, tell me, Na-Baron, what will you do, when the rumor spreads that you have been bewitched by a Bene Gesserit acolyte? You may want to think a little longer, past your first idea of a glorious butchery."
response.subject: [27.06.10199] You did what now?

response.message:
“I find the very suggestion that my loyalty to my house could be compromised extremely insulting,” Feyd-Rautha said sharply. “You may advise me, of course, but… Have we really fallen on such sad times that the heir of the house must grovel before lesser branches? I don’t think so.”

He was always keeping an especially close eye on his relatives: thwarting some, throwing crumbs to others, striving to keep alive that spirit of healthy rivalry and intrigue and mutual hatred that kept the family vigorous but harmless. Then, there were also allies and subordinate minor houses. Then, lower again, commoners allowed to get rich on Harkonnen’s sufferance (under the constant threat of retracting this privilege). The war enhanced the usual constant reshuffling on the lower levels, some of it reaching up higher, but the main structure remained relatively stable.

Could the old monster be losing the reins? Despite certain respect Feyd held for his uncle’s leadership in these troubling times and the deal they had made (the ceasing of assassination attempts in exchange for forgiveness for previous attempts and a vague promise to resign one day), the temptation to hasten his succession was always there.

There was his uncle’s intrinsic distrust of Bene Gesserit to consider, too, but as far as Feyd understood, the Baron was (with certain precautions, of course, but that was to be expected) ready to admit Ariste into household: the glee of Harkonnens getting possession of Duke’s treasure outweighed the concerns about her witch training. With that, would uncle really blame Feyd for wanting no more than he was already promised? Feyd-Rautha was not supposed to bite the hand that had plucked him from the obscurity his parents intended him for, but he was supposed to have sharp teeth. And he was not his brother, Feyd would not just stand aside meekly and allow himself to be trampled. If his uncle came to distrust him, that would quickly get messy for everyone involved (and for many unlucky uninvolved).

“I prefer to consider the bigger picture. The one that reaches Kaitain, for example. Do you think that the Emperor would be more amenable to us if he saw us making our own way out of the stalemate he put us in?” It was no big secret that Atreides on the verge of extermination and Harkonnens under the threat of bankruptcy pleased the Emperor equally. No secret, either, that he liked Atreides more but would support Harkonnens if pushed to choose. The threat of the marriage and the following truce actually happening might prove enough, the marriage itself might not even be necessary. Still, Feyd would prefer it to happen for… reasons. Many reasons, including, but not limited to how Ariste’s chest heaved under these baggy layered clothes, or how he longed to press his mouth to the tender nape of her neck, left exposed by short unruly hair, or how she looked at him when they talked... He was excited, fascinated, even, but calling it “bewitchment” would have been stupid, and he saw no reason to tolerate stupidity in the house that one day would be his.

He told Piter as much. “Butchery seems an appropriate response to preposterous slander.”

Feyd could be subtler when he wanted. When it came to actual enemies instead of entertainment, he preferred to ruin lives, not merely bodies (then again, it all came down to balancing the cost and the value).

“Before it comes to this… Well, I can give them something else to chew on.” He smiled. Bread and circuses worked not only for pyons. “For example, there’s this arena in Neo-Carthag, you know which one, Maksim Dubrov from the Mantrap runs it. Could you ensure it is not suppressed too soon? I have plans.” On Giedi Prime and the worlds ruled from there, the arenas were respectable establishments, caretakers of the sacred tradition. On Arrakis, under the damnable Guild Peace and the watchful eye of Fenring, Harkonnens had to limit themselves (at least, officially) to rare sanctioned performances.
response.subject: [27.06.10199] You did what now?

response.message:
Piter sighed. He saw that there was no point in talking to the boy. As usual, the young na-Baron was doing things his own way and was refusing to admit that his way was a product of teenage hormones rather than careful consideration. It was not without its charm, of course. A bold and careless young lad appearing at the steps of the damsel’s bedchamber, defying all the hurdles her strict father had set (presumably) for him—it was something out of an old fairy tale, and a girl as young as Ariste Aitreides could find it romantic. Alas, an old cynic like Piter saw it differently.

This marriage, if done wrong, would be even more disastrous than the war itself. It had to happen on very specific terms that he and Thufir had been going over for months before one unfortunate bull had drowned all their efforts in its blood. Romance, childish stupidity, and most importantly, feelings could not be mixed into this deal under any circumstances. Because nothing could be more easily manipulated than feelings, and no one could do it better than the Bene Gesserit.

How could he explain this all to the boy? He was afraid he could not, because he could read on the smug young face that it was already too late.

“I need to see where Thufir stands on our agreements,” Piter noted. “If he and Jessica have caught wind of this, they will start scheming. They’ll teach the little witch to ask for ‘gifts’ and ‘favors’.”

This was no good. The agreement had been originally made out of desperation. Not theirs, of course, but that of the Atreides. They had agreed to give their precious little child away only because they had no money, no plan, and no hope.

Now the na-Baron was giving House Atreides hope and, at the same time, was giving everyone else the understanding that House Harkonnen was not entirely built of ruthless, greedy monsters who could not be swayed with anything but fear. A realization that, in some not-too-distant future, the house will be controlled by a young boy who can be charmed by a siren song. A very, very dangerous notion and, unfortunately, not a wrong one.

What could Piter do about it? If it were up to him, he would probably start mixing some harmless drugs into the boy’s food to make his body forget its never-ending needs. But the Baron was strictly against it. He remembered himself at this age and he believed that his nephew, one day, would be smart enough to separate sex from politics. Piter had his doubts. He also remembered the Baron, not in his twenties, but in his thirties, and he could see the difference. Never in a million years would it have occurred to the Baron to go chasing after some pretty lordling in another city. He had always been content enough with buying all his pleasures on the slave market. The idea of talking to them beyond giving simple commands had never crossed his mind also. And the only man who was different was loyal to him to the bone (and was also his legal property).

Alas, Feyd-Rautha was not like his uncle, but like his father in this regard, it seemed. But this was also not something Piter was eager to say out loud, because he could predict the reaction—he would have to dodge a dagger or a poisoned dart. Teenagers!

He shook his head instead. Silently again. Sometimes silences worked on Feyd-Rautha when all the words did not. But, then again, sometimes not.

“I was not planning to close it. Some bored aristocrats have poured a small fortune into building the arena. All those gas traps and radiation shields. We have already agreed that the show will run at least for three full tournament seasons. Fenring’s people are informed and bribed properly. The stage is yours, na-Baron.”

He made a mock half-bow.
response.subject: [27.06.10199] You did what now?

response.message:
"Radiation shields?" said Feyd-Rautha, pleasantly surprised. "Good. Good. They must be craving for entertainment on this dull planet and I will give them the show of their lives. Of course, my anonymity must stay uncompromised until the grand finale." He smiled dreamily, anticipating the bloodshed and new adventure. Feyd had enough sense not to step into Arrakeen in near future (unless an official business happened, of course), so he wanted something else to occupy himself with. He had entered competitions on Giedi Prime incognito before, but few if any would expect him here, on Arrakis. He would hide his face and invent a flowery pseudonym. No arranged fights with ensured victory, but a real risk against whatever rubble Arrakis can offer: for all his faults that brought him here, at least Maxim knew how to stage a show, so he’d make a more or less decent pick of fighters.

If only Feyd could lure Ariste to Giedi Prime, she would understand quickly, and then learn. He’d keep her if she is a quick learner; she must be.

For Harkonnens casual cruelty to those beneath them was the natural state of things. A simple – or complicated – killing would not touch their nerves, only tickle them, at best. Watching blood being spilled was like enjoying a glass of good wine for them, every Harkonnen stranded on Arrakis would hurry to the arena to watch the fight of the new star, the… Masked Shadow? Veiled Killer? No, that part needed more work. He'd decide on the name later. Anyway, they would come and watch him dance in blood, believing themselves perfectly separated from the dirt below, cozy and safe.

Then would the great mystery unfold and Feyd-Rautha reveal his face. The revelation would hit: they were not safe, had never been safe and would never be. The ultimate predator walked among them, and if he was willing to risk his own neck just for entertainment, what were his necks for him? Exactly, nothing. That would get them, grip them like true art should. Someone would surely record his performance and send it to the Baron. Feyd knew the old fool liked watching him and imagining himself young again (and he made a conscious effort to not imagine what else the old man might be imagining).

"By the way, do you plan to punish Gurney Halleck or should I entrust it to Simone?"

Had Harkonnens been able to eliminate one of Duke’s most trusted lieutenants, they already would have. Still, an attempt on the life of Harkonnen heir was made. At least some retaliation was in order, something to make the Atreides (and Halleck especially) hurt. Simone von Konig, a sharp and vicious woman, was one of the best mentats (second-best or near enough) in Harkonnen service, and so far the most successful of all whom Feyd had tested against Piter. He did not seek to eliminate Piter (at least not yet), but he knew one day he would require his replacement, and what better way there was to prepare one? And Piter seemed to be entertained by Simone’s attempts, so, win-win.
response.subject: [27.06.10199] You did what now?

response.message:
There was a thousand ways for the Na-Baron to loose his head, but, paradoxically, being brutally chopped into pieces or gunned down in a fighting pit was not one of them. He had been proving it again and again since he had not been even fifteen - his reflexes were much sharper than his reasoning ever was. As long as it were bandits and mercenaries Feyd-Rautha was dealing with, not courtesans with gauzy skirts, Piter had nothing to worry about. 

The same applied to mortal traps in burning ships. Halleck was a complete idiot if he thought a boy who had been fighting to the death since he was strong enough to wield a dagger could fall for something so trivial. If it were Hawat's work, Piter would have suspected a smarter game here, but Halleck was just a former slave. Expecting good judgement from him would be demanding too much of the poor thing.

Piter considered for a moment what to do with him.

"Simone has no sense of humour," he sighed finally. He found it quite disappointing. It was a common flaw of all the normal mentats, and still he was unhappy that Simone had it too. "And the man does not deserve to be taken seriously."

He added meaning that starting another round of mutual killing right now was not to their favor. Especially of the young lover was planning to show up in the stronghold of his beloved again. Of course he was.

"I suggest you ask your brother to talk to his connections in the desert. Let them send some slave catchers after him. Give them a list of escaped slaves. Not the names, it would be too vulgar. Just the serial numbers. They will not achieve the goal, of course, but, when the list is found, it will send quite a message. I would bet a month-worth ration of spice that Halleck still remembers his serial number by heart."

Piter smiled.

"And we will have enough deniability for the count Fenring to smirk and look another way," he added to himself.
